title: Interference of speech and interior noise of Chinese high-speed trains with task performance
research_question: How does the combination of interior noise from Chinese high-speed trains and passengers' chatting affect task performance, emotional state, and noise annoyance?

participants.description: 83 subjects (37 females, 46 males), 46 Chinese mother tongue, 37 Dutch mother tongue. Average age 25.0 years (SD = 4.3). All lived in Belgium, were students (26 bachelor, 57 postgraduate), and reported normal hearing ability. Participants fluent in both Dutch and Chinese were excluded.
participants.recruitment: Advertisements on the university's bulletin boards

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Binaural audio stimuli combining recorded Chinese high-speed train noise (at 250 km/h and 330 km/h) with simulated speech fragments (Dutch or Chinese language, 'near' or 'far' source positions). A baseline condition of white noise at low sound pressure level was also included. Train noise recorded in an empty compartment with B&K HATS. Speech recorded in an anechoic room and simulated in a train compartment model (Odeon software).

measures.instrument: Mental arithmetic task (sum of 11 single-digit numbers)
Sentence recall task (remembering sentences, identifying previously seen sentences)
Time taken to complete calculation sums or memory recall decisions (exact clicking times registered)
Correct answer rate for calculation and memory tasks
5-point scale rating after each task part
Semantic differential combined with emotion manikins (relaxed-excited, pleased-annoyed, 5-point scale) [45, 46]
5-point scale rating (general) and forced-choice question ('Which noise made you feel more annoying? Train noise, speech noise, or equally annoying?')
Estimated duration of auditory attention attracted by background sound, using a saliency-based notice-event model [35, 47]

findings.consequent: Correct answer rate for calculation task
findings.quote: No effect of test condition on task accuracy was found.

findings.consequent: Correct answer rate for memory task recall
findings.quote: The correct answer rates for the recall part of the memory task (0.52±0.08, 0.52±0.08, 0.51±0.07 and 0.53±0.09) also did not show significant differences.

findings.mechanism: Sound environment influenced task duration rather than task accuracy.
findings.quote: Overall, it can be concluded that, in the present experiment, a change in sound environment influenced task duration rather than task accuracy
For the calculation task, an independent samples student t-test showed that the participants do not respond significantly slower or faster when train speed is varied.

findings.antecedent: Background noise containing speech (S250farDut, S250farChn) compared to train noise only (S250train) at 250 km/h, far position
findings.consequent: Answering time for calculation task (Chinese-speaking participants)
findings.quote: Results are listed for 50% and 100% completion of the test. The first three rows of Table 3 show results for a train speed of 250 km/h and with the listener in the far position. It can be seen that, in this case, presenting speech facilitates the task: both the Dutch-speaking and the Chinese-speaking participants show a reduced answering time when the background noise contains language elements. Results are analyzed statistically using a pairwise t-test. It was found that the differences in answering times are only significant (p < 0.05) for the Chinese-speaking group.

findings.antecedent: Background noise containing speech (S250farDut, S250farChn) compared to train noise only (S250train) at 250 km/h, far position
findings.consequent: Answering time for calculation task (Dutch-speaking participants)
findings.quote: No significant effect of speech language is found.

findings.antecedent: Interfering speech in participant's mother tongue (S250nearDut for Dutch, S250nearChn for Chinese) compared to train noise only (S250train) at 250 km/h, near position
findings.mechanism: Higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for near position leads to higher interfering effect of speech.
findings.quote: In this case, presenting speech reduces the calculation speed, but effects are only significant (p < 0.05) when the language of the interfering speech equals the participants mother tongue.

findings.antecedent: Higher train noise level (330 km/h) compared to lower train noise level (250 km/h)
findings.consequent: Effect of speech on calculation speed
findings.mechanism: Higher train noise level results in a lower SNR, masking the speech effect.
findings.quote: On the one hand, it can be seen that, in this case, the effect of the speech disappears, because the higher train noise level results in a lower SNR. On the other hand, it is clear from Table 3 that the higher overall noise level does not affect response times.

findings.antecedent: Basic acoustical parameters (LAeq, LA10, SNR of speech)
findings.consequent: Response time (relative to baseline) for calculation task
findings.mechanism: These parameters can only partially explain observed variance; a more in-depth analysis of background noise is needed.
findings.quote: It can be seen that the selected acoustical parameters can only partially explain the observed variance in response time; no significant (linear) relationship can be discerned.

findings.antecedent: Estimated duration of auditory attention attracted by background sound (from saliency-based notice-event model)
findings.mechanism: The more attention is paid to the noise as predicted by the model, the lower the normalized progress, meaning participants need more time to respond. This indicates the attention model is a good predictor for response times.
findings.quote: First, at each of the four time instances within the task, the same trend is visible: the more attention is paid to the noise as predicted by the model, the lower the normalized progress is, which means the participants need more time to respond. This indicates that the attention estimated using the notice-event model could be a good predictor for response times.

findings.antecedent: Increasing time within the task (exposure duration)
findings.consequent: Slope of the regressed line between estimated auditory attention and calculation speed
findings.mechanism: Participants were gradually becoming used to the background noise (habituation).
findings.quote: Second, with increasing time within the task, the slope of the regressed line decreases. This could indicate that the participants were gradually becoming used to the background noise.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to train noise (CTrain, CDutch, CChinese conditions) compared to baseline (CBaseline)
findings.mechanism: Persistent exposure to noise and related task interference might have an adverse impact on perceived well-being.
findings.quote: A t-test reveals that participants are significantly less pleased after exposure to either of the stimuli of the CTrain, CDutch or CChinese conditions (p < 0.001), compared to baseline condition

findings.antecedent: Composition of background noise (CTrain, CDutch, CChinese)
findings.quote: but no significant differences were found between any of the combinations, CTrain and CDutch/CChinese, with p > 0.1.

findings.mechanism: Sound characteristics and meaning play an important role in perceived annoyance, even under a considerably higher sound level of train noise.
findings.quote: Nevertheless, as much as 22 % found the speech noise to be more annoying, and only 7% found the train noise to be more annoying. This result somewhat contrasts the findings obtained through the emotional manikins, and indicates that, even under a background noise with a considerably higher sound level, interfering speech can still lead to a higher annoyance.
Most participants (71%) felt that the train noise and the speech were about equally annoying.

mechanisms: Distracting effect of speech on cognitive task performance.
Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between speech and train sound influencing the interfering effect of speech.
Masking of interfering speech by higher train noise levels.
Saliency of sound features (spectro-temporal changes) attracting attention, even at low sound levels.
Habituation to constant broadband noise over time.
Sound characteristics and meaning playing an important role in perceived annoyance, even when speech levels are low relative to background noise.
moderators: Language of interfering speech (matching participant's mother tongue)
Distance between speech source and receiver (affecting SNR)
implementation_implications: Lowering only the sound level of train noise may not be beneficial, as people might still be disturbed by interfering speech.
Design considerations should account for the distracting nature of speech and its impact on task performance, especially when the speech is in the listener's native language.
The importance of sound characteristics and meaning in perceived annoyance suggests that noise control strategies should go beyond simple sound level reduction.

tables.description: Composition of the experimental menus, together with the main acoustical parameters of the experimental stimuli (energetic averages between left and right ear).
Pearson's correlation (and associated p-value) between response duration and accuracy, considering the different experimental conditions and task types separately.

Duration within the calculation task, for 50% and 100% completion of the task, where "*" indicates statistical significant difference compared to the sample without speech in the same group of 3 stimuli (p < 0.05). Standard deviations are shown inside parentheses.

limitations: The assessment of emotional state or well-being during the test was not very subtle, potentially missing subtle differences between different types of noise.
Response times for the recall parts of the memory task were considerably influenced by participants' typing ability and the length of the answer, making detailed analysis of these results difficult.
The influence of the visual setting, which could have a mediating effect on annoyance, was neglected.
